For each integer \(n\ge2\), let \(\mathcal K_n\) consist of all sets \(K=\overline\Omega\subset\mathbb C^n\), where \(\Omega\) is a nonempty bounded connected open set with \(C^\infty\) boundary.

Use the following orientation convention for pseudoconvexity. Near each \(q\in\partial K\), take a smooth real defining function \(\rho\) with \(K\cap U=\{\rho\le0\}\) and \(d\rho\ne0\) on \(\partial K\cap U\). The boundary \(\partial K\) is pseudoconvex if, at every such \(q\),
\[
\sum_{j,k=1}^{n}\rho_{z_j\bar z_k}(q)v_j\overline{v_k}\ge0
\qquad\text{whenever}\qquad
\sum_{j=1}^{n}\rho_{z_j}(q)v_j=0.
\]

An open set \(Y\subset\mathbb C^n\) is called Oka if, for every integer \(m\ge1\), every nonempty compact convex set \(Q\subset\mathbb C^m\), every holomorphic map \(f:V\to Y\) on an open neighbourhood \(V\) of \(Q\), and every \(\varepsilon>0\), there is a holomorphic map \(F:\mathbb C^m\to Y\) satisfying
\[
\sup_{x\in Q}\|F(x)-f(x)\|<\varepsilon,
\]
where the norm is Euclidean.

Define the two sets of dimensions
\[
\begin{aligned}
S&=\bigl\{n\in\mathbb Z_{\ge2}:\ \text{for every }K\in\mathcal K_n,\quad
\partial K\text{ pseudoconvex}\ \Longrightarrow\ \mathbb C^n\setminus K\text{ Oka}\bigr\},\\
N&=\bigl\{n\in\mathbb Z_{\ge2}:\ \text{for every }K\in\mathcal K_n,\quad
\mathbb C^n\setminus K\text{ Oka}\ \Longrightarrow\ \partial K\text{ pseudoconvex}\bigr\}.
\end{aligned}
\]
Determine exactly the ordered pair \((S,N)\).

\[
K\subset\mathbb C^n\ \text{compact and polynomially convex},\quad n\ge2
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
\mathbb C^n\setminus K\ \text{is Oka}.
\]
One cannot replace “polynomially convex” here by “the closure of a smoothly bounded pseudoconvex domain” as an established general theorem. Smooth pseudoconvexity does not imply polynomial convexity; it does not even guarantee a Stein neighbourhood basis. Thus this theorem does not determine \(S\) in the question.

\[
2\in N.

The proof has two elementary analytic ingredients.

Let \(Y\) satisfy the problem’s Oka approximation property, and let \(u:Y\to\mathbb R\) be continuous, plurisubharmonic, and bounded above.

Take any sufficiently small affine disc
\[
f(\zeta)=p+\zeta v
\]
whose image on a neighbourhood of \(\overline{\mathbb D}\) lies in \(Y\). Applying the definition with \(m=1\) and \(Q=\overline{\mathbb D}\), obtain entire maps \(F_j:\mathbb C\to Y\) converging uniformly to \(f\) on \(\overline{\mathbb D}\).

Each \(u\circ F_j\) is a bounded-above subharmonic function on \(\mathbb C\), hence constant by subharmonic Liouville. Continuity of \(u\) gives, for every \(\zeta\in\overline{\mathbb D}\),
\[
u(f(\zeta))
=\lim_j u(F_j(\zeta))
=\lim_j u(F_j(0))
=u(f(0)).
\]
Therefore \(u\) is constant on every sufficiently small affine disc, and so locally constant on \(Y\). No connectedness assumption on the whole exterior is needed.

Strict positivity of the Levi form on \(\ker\partial r(0)\) implies that, for sufficiently large \(A>0\),
\[
R=r+Ar^2
\]
has positive-definite full complex Hessian at \(0\). Indeed,
\[
R_{j\bar k}(0)=r_{j\bar k}(0)+2A\,r_j(0)r_{\bar k}(0),

\quad\text{on }\overline Y\cap B_\delta.

The relevant necessary-condition theorem is:

> **Stein-neighbourhood obstruction.** Let \(K\subset\mathbb C^n\), \(n\ge2\), be the closure of a bounded domain with smooth boundary. If \(\mathbb C^n\setminus K\) is Oka, then \(K\) has a Stein neighbourhood basis.

Here Oka can equivalently be defined by the convex approximation property in the question. This theorem is substantially stronger than the elementary obstruction coming from bounded plurisubharmonic functions.

### 2. Consequently, every dimension belongs to \(N\)

A smoothly bounded compact domain having a Stein neighbourhood basis has pseudoconvex boundary.

Indeed, suppose its defining function \(\rho\) has a negative tangential Levi direction at a boundary point. The standard local Hartogs-figure argument then supplies a compact Hartogs figure inside \(\Omega\) whose holomorphic filling crosses \(\partial\Omega\). Every Stein neighbourhood of \(K\) must contain that filling, by the continuity principle. Thus Stein neighbourhoods cannot shrink arbitrarily closely to \(K\), a contradiction.

Applying the compact-obstacle theorem gives, in every dimension \(n\ge2\),
\[
\mathbb C^n\setminus K\text{ Oka}
\ \Longrightarrow\
K\text{ has a Stein neighbourhood basis}
\ \Longrightarrow\
\partial K\text{ pseudoconvex}.
\]
Therefore
\[
N=\mathbb Z_{\ge2}.
\]

Start with a smoothly bounded pseudoconvex worm domain
\[
D\Subset\mathbb C^2
\]
whose closure has no Stein neighbourhood basis. Its complement cannot be Oka, by the same necessary-condition theorem. This already excludes \(2\) from \(S\).

For completeness, this obstruction can be carried into every higher dimension while retaining smooth pseudoconvex boundary.

Choose a smooth defining function \(r\) for \(D\) such that
\[
-\log(-r)
\]
is plurisubharmonic on \(D\). Such a choice follows from a Diederich–Fornæss defining function. For \(n>2\), put
\[
D_n=\left\{(z,w)\in D\times\mathbb C^{\,n-2}:
\|w\|^2<-r(z)\right\}.
\]
This is bounded and connected. Its boundary is smooth: where \(w\ne0\), the \(w\)-gradient is nonzero, while where \(w=0\) on the boundary, \(dr\ne0\).

It is also pseudoconvex. Away from \(w=0\), it is defined by the negative sublevel set of the plurisubharmonic function
\[
\log\|w\|^2-\log(-r(z));
\]
pseudoconvexity at the remaining boundary points follows by continuity of the tangential Levi form.

Finally,
\[
\overline{D_n}\cap
\bigl(\mathbb C^2\times\{0\}\bigr)
=\overline D.
\]
If \(\overline{D_n}\) had a Stein neighbourhood basis, intersecting those neighbourhoods with the closed complex subspace \(\mathbb C^2\times\{0\}\) would give a Stein neighbourhood basis of \(\overline D\), a contradiction.

Thus \(\overline{D_n}\) has smooth pseudoconvex boundary but non-Oka complement for every \(n\ge2\). Hence \(S=\varnothing\), yielding the displayed pair.

Choose a nonconstant affine holomorphic disk \(f\), defined near \(Q=\overline{\mathbb D}\), with \(f(Q)\Subset W\). Choose an approximation tolerance sufficiently small that any approximant \(F\) satisfies both:

If \(Y\) had the stated CAP, such an entire \(F:\mathbb C\to Y\) would exist. But \(u\circ F\) is bounded and subharmonic on \(\mathbb C\), hence constant. On \(\mathbb D\),
\[
\partial_t\partial_{\bar t}(u\circ F)
=\mathcal L_u(F(t);F'(t)).
\]
Strict positivity of the Levi form on \(W\) forces \(F'=0\) there. The identity theorem makes \(F\) constant everywhere, a contradiction.

This argument needs neither connectedness of \(Y\) nor any smoothness of \(u\) outside \(W\).

### 2. A strictly pseudoconvex boundary point produces such a function

Let \(q\in\partial Y\) be a smooth strictly pseudoconvex boundary point, with local defining function \(r\), oriented so that \(Y=\{r<0\}\).

For sufficiently large \(A>0\),
\[
\widetilde r=r+Ar^2
\]
is strictly plurisubharmonic near \(q\), and has the same sign as \(r\) after shrinking the neighborhood. The key identity is
\[
\mathcal L_{\widetilde r}
=(1+2Ar)\mathcal L_r+2A|\partial r|^2.
\]
At the boundary, the added rank-one term supplies positivity in the complex normal direction; tangential positivity is already available.

\[
\phi=\widetilde r-\epsilon\|z-q\|^2

\[
\phi<0,\qquad
\phi\le-\epsilon R^2
\quad\text{on }Y\cap\partial B(q,R).
\]
Set \(c=-\epsilon R^2/2\) and define
\[
u(z)=
\begin{cases}
\max\{\phi(z),c\},&z\in Y\cap B(q,R),\\
c,&z\in Y\setminus B(q,R).
\end{cases}
\]
The strict inequality on the spherical edge ensures valid gluing: locally near that edge, the maximum equals the constant. Thus \(u\) is bounded, continuous, and plurisubharmonic globally on \(Y\).

The latest reports expose a gap in my previous answer. I asserted the implication
\[
\mathbb C^n\setminus K\text{ Oka}
\Longrightarrow K\text{ has a Stein neighbourhood basis}
\]
as a theorem without substantiating it. That was unjustified. I withdraw both that assertion and the resulting ordered pair.

The rigorous dimension-set conclusion established here is
\[
\boxed{2\in N}.
\]

Here is a concise proof directly from the approximation definition.

First, a continuous bounded-above plurisubharmonic function \(u\) on an Oka open set \(Y\) must be locally constant. Indeed, approximate a small affine holomorphic disc \(f\) in \(Y\) uniformly by entire maps \(F_j:\mathbb C\to Y\). Each \(u\circ F_j\) is bounded-above subharmonic on \(\mathbb C\), hence constant. Continuity then shows that \(u\circ f\) is constant.

Next, suppose \(Y\) has a smooth strongly pseudoconvex boundary point \(q\). Take a local defining function \(r<0\) on \(Y\). For sufficiently large \(A\),
\[
s=r+Ar^2
\]
is strictly plurisubharmonic near \(q\) and remains negative on the nearby part of \(Y\). For sufficiently small \(\eta>0\),
\[
h=s-\eta\|z-q\|^2
\]
is still strictly plurisubharmonic and satisfies
\[
h\le-\eta\|z-q\|^2.
\]
On a small ball \(B(q,R)\), choose \(0<c<\eta R^2\). The function
\[
u(z)=
\begin{cases}
\max\{h(z),-c\},&z\in Y\cap B(q,R),\\
-c,&z\in Y\setminus B(q,R)
\end{cases}
\]
glues validly across the artificial spherical boundary. It is bounded, continuous and plurisubharmonic, and is strictly plurisubharmonic on a nonempty cap approaching \(q\). Thus it is not locally constant, contradicting Okaness.

Finally, in complex dimension two, failure of the stated pseudoconvexity condition means that the obstacle’s Levi form is negative definite on its one-dimensional complex tangent space at some point. Reversing orientation gives a strongly pseudoconvex boundary point of the exterior. Consequently,
\[
\mathbb C^2\setminus K\text{ Oka}
\Longrightarrow \partial K\text{ pseudoconvex}.
\]

The worms without Stein neighbourhood bases do **not**, without the missing bridge, establish \(S=\varnothing\). Likewise, the mixed-Levi examples do not establish failure of necessity in higher dimensions. I therefore do not have a complete determination of \((S,N)\); neither of my previously asserted exact conclusions was justified.
